The codpiece was a covering or protrusion added to the front of men's breeches or hose, worn from the fifteenth through seventeenth centuries. What began as a practical closure for fitted legwear evolved into an ostentatiously padded and ornamented garment, making it one of history's boldest displays of masculine status and virility.

Originally just a simple laced or tied opening in fitted hose, the codpiece became increasingly visible and prominent during the Renaissance. It reached its maximum size and decoration in the sixteenth century, when padded and jeweled codpieces signaled wealth, power, and masculine assertion. The garment was stuffed with wool, horse hair, or other materials to create an exaggerated bulge. The most extreme versions protruded dramatically from the body, sometimes elaborately embroidered, slashed to reveal colored silk beneath, or studded with jewels. Some codpieces doubled as decorative pouches for coins or jewels.

The height of fashion among European nobility and wealthy merchants, the conspicuous absence of codpieces in the lower classes reflected sumptuary laws that restricted ornamentation. The codpiece was associated with Renaissance ideals of male display and conquest, simultaneously functional and a declaration of masculine virility and status. It declined by the early sixteen hundreds as silhouettes shifted and men's fashion moved toward longer coat designs that obscured the lower body.

The codpiece shares its cultural moment with the ruff, the contemporary elaborate neckwear that shared the Renaissance ethos of bold, ornamented display. It stands as the masculine counterpart to the farthingale, women's equivalent in terms of extravagant structural undergarment signaling status and fashion authority. The codpiece's popularity and acceptance at court reflected the aesthetic ideals of Henry VIII, the English king whose court exemplified the opulent, masculine codpiece aesthetic of the Renaissance, an era of humanist celebration of the male form and display of individual status.
